system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

Chapter 5: Improving your Blues Ideas

<<<CHAPTER FILE
# Chapter 5 — Improving your Blues Ideas

_Pages 183-243._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## Licks as musical words

> Now that you have a basic understanding of how to play over the blues, let's learn some pre-set
>   small musical ideas that we will call: “licks”. They are like words that we learn and
>   memorize just like when we start speaking a language. In order to make this process easier,
>   much more interesting and cooler, let’s play these licks over a rhythm called the boogaloo:

**Significance (p. 183).** Defines 'licks' via language analogy and frames the boogaloo as the practice rhythm.

## Choosing fingering/picking based on context

> Below we have many options of fingering and picking possibilities for these licks. You can
> choose one of the examples depending on where you are coming from or going to on the guitar
> fretboard.

**Significance (p. 184).** Context-driven fingering rule: pick the option based on surrounding fretboard motion.

## Minor blues substitution tricks

> After learning some major blues licks, now it is time to learn some minor ideas that can be
>  used over the minor blues. But be careful, because the minor blues form has two different
>  types of chords (minor and dominant), so we must learn some substitution tricks before
>  we start (Cm key):

**Significance (p. 195).** Sets up the substitution-tricks framework needed because minor blues mixes minor and dominant chords.

## Memorize substitutions without theory

> Notice that by doing this type of substitution, depending on the lick we might have some notes
> that are not derived from the simple chords Ab7 or G7. But for now, it is not necessary to
> understand the theory behind it, just memorize them.

**Significance (p. 195).** Pedagogical rule: memorize first, theorize later, even when notes don't derive from underlying chords.

## Extended blues licks work over any chord

> Next, we have many examples of extended blues licks in the key of “C”. It is important to
> understand that in theory, we could use all of them over any major or minor chord, because
> we are talking about the blues.

**Significance (p. 210).** Establishes the universal applicability of extended blues licks across major and minor chords.

## Pure minor pentatonic over minor family

> However, when the melodic line is built from the minor pentatonic scale without any
> mixture of the major pentatonic scale, our preference is to use the lines over minor chords
> or chord sequences belonging to the "minor chord family" (natural minor harmonic Eield).

**Significance (p. 210).** Preference rule: unmixed minor pentatonic lines belong over the minor chord family.

## Minor pentatonic over major chords

> This is not a rule. Melodic lines using only the minor pentatonic scale will often work
> perfectly over major chords such as C6, Cmaj7 and of course C7.

**Significance (p. 210).** Counterpoint: minor pentatonic works over C6/Cmaj7/C7, so the previous preference isn't absolute.

## Lick chord-context labels

> In the begining of each melodic line we have given some chord possibilities that these lines
> will work over. Remember that blues lines work differently than other types of lines, as
> they can be played in many different harmonic situations.

**Significance (p. 210).** Reading aid: each line's chord-labels are suggestions because blues lines float across many harmonic contexts.

## Singing licks to internalize them

> The secret to mastering when and where to use these melodic lines is quite simple: learn to
> sing every melodic line (lick) that you know. Internalize the sound. If you do this, as time
> goes by things will become easier and you will know exactly when and where to use them.

**Significance (p. 210).** Method's core rule for lick mastery: sing first, internalize the sound, application follows.

## Fingering & picking must be followed exactly

> Note: When studing the melodic lines, never forget the importance of connecting both
> hands. So follow the given Eingering & picking possibilities exactly as notated for each one
> of the examples.

**Significance (p. 210).** Reinforces the method's core rule that notated fingering and picking are not arbitrary.

CHAPTER FILE>>>
